ety.text: From Middle English mase, from Middle English masen (“to perplex, bewilder”); or perhaps from Old English *mæs (“delusion, bewilderment”); akin to Old English āmasian (“to perplex, confound”), Icelandic masa (“to chatter”). More at amaze.

senses.d: A labyrinth; a puzzle consisting of a complicated network of paths or passages, the aim of which is to find one's way through.
Something made up of many confused or conflicting elements; a tangle.
ex: The project developer, Poseidon Resources Corp., has been winding its way through a maze of state and local agencies for six years

senses.d: A confusion of thought; a state of bewilderment.

ex: they so mazed and even stupified his Conscience
mazed […] by the eyes of the crowd
She rowed back alone, the simple soul that was in her forwandered and mazed with excess of joy.

ety.text: Attested 1604 in Antoine de Montchrestien. From Middle French dedalus after Dédale (“Daedalus”), who built the Cretan Labyrinth in Greek mythology, from Latin Daedalus, from Ancient Greek Δαίδαλος (Daídalos).

chain.g: a building with many winding passages, a labyrinth; especially that built by Daedalus, near Knossos, Crete

ety.text: From Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λαβύρινθος (labúrinthos).
